items.title: Stanley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998
items.q: So after that we agreed to be married, and Helen came to England and we lived there about twelve years.

ctx.x: I think I heard that — with Lester Young on it?

Yeah, it’s quite recent. Well that was different you know. This is a different audience and element. I mean you’d go to the Savoy Ballroom or places like that, there would be applause. But it wasn’t hysterical in the way it seemed to me. But fortunately, we turned to Ellington. He did a concert while I was there, it was the “Deep South Suite,” and that sort of confirmed to me that the battle wasn’t lost. So after that we agreed to be married, and Helen came to England and we lived there about twelve years.
Did you two meet on your first visit?

items.title: Helen Oakley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998
items.q: And so Stanley helped me, you know, he would criticize.

ctx.x: You know it was almost like a novel, and I knew the ending, but I wanted to say to T- Bone like don’t take that drink, you know, don’t— you wanted to — such a life, such a blues life.

I’m so glad that you liked him, because Stanley will contradict me, but the fact was that Stanley didn’t like it. I hadn’t done a book before, I’d done writing you know. And so Stanley helped me, you know, he would criticize. Criticize is the word, always, isn’t he a critic? And so it was different from anything that he’s critiqued. And I knew he didn’t think too much of it. And so I wasn’t too sure myself. But the people in Louisiana, the

press, were very nice. And they loved it. And a reader, she said, “I’m writing you this letter because it moved me.” The reader said, “I’ve never read anything that moved me so much, and I cried both times I read it.”
